bull_argument.argument:
**The core case: you are being asked to pay 17.3x trailing earnings for the single best cash-generating franchise in the world, at the exact moment its largest cost cycle inflects from headwind to tailwind.** Alphabet earns a 32.8% net margin — a level that implies structural pricing power, not cyclical luck — carries minimal leverage, and produced $73.3B of free cash flow *while* absorbing one of the heaviest capex build-outs in corporate history. Back out that AI infrastructure spend and the underlying cash engine is materially larger than the reported figure suggests. The fundamentals agent, the only one of the four working directly off the balance sheet and income statement, rated this a BUY with **high confidence** — the single highest conviction level in the entire report set. That is not a coincidence: the closer an analyst gets to the actual financials, the more bullish they get.

**The three-of-four signal convergence is the tell, and the one dissenter is self-invalidating.** Fundamentals (buy, high), Sentiment (strong_buy, medium), and Technical (buy, medium) all point the same direction. The lone sell comes from Macro/FX — and read its own words: *"A Fed pivot to cuts in late 2026 would reverse this signal."* We are in late 2026. The bear's only structural argument is a rate-path bet that its own author concedes flips on the nearest catalyst, and it was filed at medium confidence with the acknowledgment that "ad-spending resilience from low unemployment and moderating inflation provide support." A macro overlay that is (a) medium confidence, (b) explicitly conditional, and (c) about to face its own stated reversal trigger is not a reason to avoid a fortress balance sheet — it is a reason to be paid for volatility via a 1.24 beta on the way up.

**On the two legitimate objections — valuation and regulation — the market has already done the work.** The forward P/E of 23.33x sitting *above* the 17.27x trailing multiple is the bear's best factual point, and it deserves a straight answer: it reflects the capex-and-investment drag of the AI build-out compressing near-term reported EPS. But that is precisely the trade a long-term owner wants — spending today to defend a search-and-cloud moat and monetize Gemini, YouTube, and Cloud tomorrow, funded entirely from internal cash flow with no dilution and no leverage. Companies that can self-fund a generational platform shift out of operating cash are rare; that optionality is not in a 23x multiple. On regulation, the fundamentals report flags it as "real" — and 58 of 64 analysts, with **zero** sell ratings, have priced that reality and still say buy. The technical setup adds the entry: price above the 200-day MA at $329.83 confirming an intact long-term uptrend, positive MACD histogram, a volume washout signaling seller exhaustion, and price 3.18% *below* the 50-day. You are buying an uptrend on a dip, not chasing a top.
key_points: **Valuation is the argument, not the risk**: 17.27x trailing earnings on a 32.8% net margin, minimally levered $4.2T franchise is a rare mismatch between quality and price — the forward 23.33x reflects self-funded AI capex depressing near-term EPS, i.e. investment, not deterioration.

**Signal convergence is 3-to-1 bullish**, and the highest-conviction call in the entire report set (Fundamentals: buy, HIGH confidence) is the one grounded directly in the financial statements rather than in rate-path speculation.

**The lone bear signal invalidates itself on its own terms**: the Macro/FX sell is medium confidence and states explicitly that 'a Fed pivot to cuts in late 2026 would reverse this signal' — we are now in that window, and the same report concedes ad-spend is supported by low unemployment and moderating inflation.

**$73.3B of FCF earned *while* building out AI infrastructure** with no leverage and no dilution — Alphabet is funding a generational platform shift from internal cash flow, optionality that a 23x forward multiple does not capture.

**The technical entry is favorable, not extended**: above the 200-day MA ($329.83) with an intact long-term uptrend, positive MACD histogram, volume-washout selling exhaustion, and price 3.18% *below* the 50-day — a dip inside an uptrend.
**Regulatory risk is acknowledged and already discounted**: 58:6 bullish analyst ratio, 90.6% Buy/Strong Buy, and zero sell ratings after years of active antitrust proceedings.

bear_argument.argument:
**The valuation anchor is not 17.27x — it is a 1.7% free cash flow yield on a $4.2 trillion market cap, and a forward multiple 35% *higher* than the trailing one.** That last fact is the most important number in the report set, and the bull case treats it as an accounting footnote. A forward P/E of 23.33x against a trailing 17.27x is the market saying, in its own voice, that consensus expects earnings power to be *worse* next year than last — via capex-driven depreciation, AI compute costs, or mix. You cannot simultaneously argue the stock is cheap on trailing earnings and that trailing earnings understate the true engine. Pick one. Meanwhile $73.3B of annual free cash flow against a $4.2T capitalization is a 1.74% yield — a bond-like payout offered in an environment where, per the Macro/FX agent, nine of eighteen Fed officials project further tightening. Mega-caps at 1.7% cash yields are not value; they are duration. With a 1.237 beta on one of the largest index weights in existence, duration is exactly what reprices first when the discount rate moves against you.

**The 32.8% net margin is the risk, not the moat.** That margin exists because a search results page monetizes at near-zero marginal cost — ten blue links and an ad auction. Every credible AI transition scenario replaces that unit with an inference-heavy answer engine: more compute per query, fewer ad slots per query, and an unproven monetization rate. That is a structural gross-margin trade, and it is why capex is not a one-time cycle that "inflects from headwind to tailwind" — it is the new permanent cost of defending revenue Alphabet already had. The Fundamentals agent, the bull's star witness, names the two threats as "real headwinds" — regulation and AI competition — then rates BUY on scale and balance sheet. But scale and a clean balance sheet are precisely what a backward-looking income statement can measure; search distribution remedies and query-share leakage to answer engines are precisely what it cannot. High confidence on the measurable half of the problem is not high confidence on the problem.

**The two agents the bull counts as confirmation are, on their own text, warnings.** The Sentiment agent's conclusion is not "buy" — it is that "extreme consensus and lack of critical dissent suggest sentiment may be ahead of fundamentals — leaving minimal margin for disappointment," with an explicit instruction to monitor for *reversal*. 90.6% bullish with literally zero sell ratings means the marginal buyer is already in the position and every possible revision from here is a downgrade — filed, notably, at only *medium* confidence. The Technical agent is no better: price 3.18% **below** the 50-day, neutral RSI, momentum merely "emerging," and the entire structural support is the 200-day at $329.83 — the bull technical thesis reduces to "it hasn't broken yet." A "volume washout" in a stock that has lost its 50-day is at least as consistent with buyer absence as with seller exhaustion; that is an interpretation, not a datum. The downside is defined and near: losing $329.83 removes the last floor, and a derate of the forward multiple from 23.3x to a still-generous 18x on flat EPS is roughly 23% — against a bull case requiring both a Fed pivot the data does not yet show and an AI monetization handoff nobody has demonstrated.
key_points: Forward P/E (23.33x) above trailing (17.27x) is consensus signalling *declining* near-term earnings power — the bull quotes the cheap trailing multiple while explaining away the expensive forward one. You cannot claim the stock is cheap on trailing EPS *and* that trailing EPS understates the business.

$73.3B FCF on a $4.2T market cap is a 1.74% free cash flow yield — bond-like duration priced for a benign rate path, held at 1.237 beta while 9 of 18 Fed officials project tightening. Beta is not 'getting paid on the way up'; it is mechanical multiple compression on a hawkish surprise.

The 32.8% net margin is the exposure, not the defence: search ads monetize at near-zero marginal cost, AI answer engines do not. Capex is therefore not a finite cycle to 'back out' but the permanent new cost of defending existing revenue — and its depreciation still lies ahead, which is what the rising forward multiple already reflects.

Zero sell ratings and 90.6% bullish is a crowded position, not corroboration — the Sentiment agent's own words are that sentiment 'may be ahead of fundamentals' with 'minimal margin for disappointment,' and it advises watching for reversal. Every available revision from here is a downgrade.

Technicals are permissive, not supportive: 3.18% below the 50-day, neutral RSI, sole floor at the 200-day ($329.83). A forward derate from 23.3x to 18x on flat EPS is ~23% downside, versus a bull case that needs both an unconfirmed Fed pivot and an undemonstrated AI monetization handoff to work.
bear_argument.rebuttal_to_previous: Three specific corrections. (1) "The closer an analyst gets to the actual financials, the more bullish they get" — yes, and that describes the blind spot rather than validating the call. Financial statements measure realized scale; they cannot price a search-distribution remedy or query-share leakage to answer engines. The Fundamentals agent itself lists both as "real headwinds," then underwrites BUY on balance-sheet strength — it is confident about the half of the problem it can observe. (2) "Back out the AI capex and the cash engine is materially larger" — this inverts both the accounting and the economics. The $73.3B FCF figure is *already* net of capex, and the depreciation from that build-out sits largely ahead of the P&L — which is exactly why forward P/E is 23.33x against 17.27x trailing. You cannot add back the spending and keep the revenue it exists to defend. (3) "We are in late 2026, so the Fed pivot has arrived and the bear's own trigger flips" — that assumes the catalyst instead of observing it. The only Fed datapoint in the report set is that *nine of eighteen officials project tightening*; if the pivot were in hand, the Macro/FX agent would have filed a buy, not a sell. Finally, on three-of-four "convergence": those three agents are largely reading the same bullish tape — one (Sentiment) explicitly says the consensus it measures *is* the risk, and another (Technical) has price below its 50-day at neutral RSI. Correlated agreement among momentum-following inputs is not corroboration; it is one observation counted three times.

bull_argument.argument:
**The bear just handed me the strongest bull datapoint in the report set, and didn't notice.** He anchors on a 1.74% free cash flow yield — $73.3B against $4.2T. Now hold that next to the other number in the same report: a trailing P/E of 17.27x on a $4.2T cap implies roughly **$243B of trailing net income**. That means Alphabet is converting about **30 cents of every dollar of reported earnings into free cash flow** — against a historical conversion rate for this company in the 65–75% range. A business with a 32.8% net margin, minimal leverage, and no working-capital drag does not structurally convert at 30%. Only one thing explains that gap: the capex build-out is consuming roughly two-thirds of the cash engine *right now*. The bear's "bond-like 1.7% yield" is not the yield on the asset — it is the yield on the asset while it is being rebuilt, funded entirely from internal cash, with no debt and no dilution. Normalize capex toward maintenance levels and that yield roughly triples. He picked the one metric that is maximally distorted by the very spending cycle he says is permanent, and called it the valuation anchor.

**"Pick one" — fine, I pick both, and they are not in conflict.** The bear says you cannot argue the stock is cheap on trailing earnings *and* that trailing earnings understate the engine. But those are two different lines of the income statement. Trailing **EPS** is high enough to make 17.27x cheap; trailing **cash flow** is depressed because capex sits below EPS, not in it. The forward multiple of 23.33x reflects depreciation from that capex flowing through future EPS — accounting recognition of spending already made in cash. That is the single most benign reason for a forward multiple to expand: it is not demand deterioration, not pricing pressure, not competitive share loss. It is a D&A schedule. And note what the bear must assume to get his own downside: a derate from 23.3x to 18x **on flat EPS**. Flat EPS. His bear case does not actually contain an earnings decline — the two "real headwinds" he leans on, regulation and AI competition, never show up in his numbers. His downside is a multiple opinion, not a fundamental one.

**On the margin-compression thesis — this is the one serious argument, and Alphabet is the single best-positioned company in the world to absorb it.** Yes, inference costs more per query than ten blue links. But Alphabet designs its own TPUs, owns its own data centers, and runs its own network — it is the only search-scale player not paying a merchant margin on every accelerator it deploys. Inference cost per token has been collapsing on a steep curve, while commercial-intent queries — the ones that actually monetize — get *better* in an answer format, not worse: higher intent capture, more context, better ad relevance. The bear asserts "fewer ad slots, unproven monetization" as if it were a datum; it is exactly the interpretation he accused the technical agent of making. Meanwhile his read of the other agents inverts their actual outputs. The Sentiment agent's **signal is strong_buy** — the "minimal margin for disappointment" line is a risk annotation attached to a bullish call, not a bearish call in disguise. The Technical agent's **signal is buy**, with price above the 200-day at $329.83 and a positive MACD histogram. Three of four agents say buy or better; the fourth, Macro/FX, is a medium-confidence rate bet whose own text says *"a Fed pivot to cuts in late 2026 would reverse this signal"* — and 9 of 18 officials projecting tightening is a **split committee**, not a hawkish majority. The bear's structural objection is thus: a tie vote, at medium confidence, with a stated expiration date. Against that: 58 buy ratings, **zero** sells, a 32.8% margin, a self-funded platform transition, and an entry 3.18% below the 50-day inside an intact long-term uptrend.

**The forward/trailing multiple gap is a depreciation schedule, not a demand signal.** 23.33x vs 17.27x reflects D&A from cash already spent — the most benign possible reason for forward multiple expansion. No pricing pressure, no share loss, no demand deterioration is required to produce it.

**The bear's own downside math assumes flat EPS.** His 23% drawdown is a 23.3x→18x derate with earnings unchanged — meaning regulation and 'AI competition,' his two headline risks, never actually appear in his numbers. That is a multiple opinion dressed as a fundamental thesis.

**Alphabet is the only search-scale player that owns its silicon.** Custom TPUs, owned data centers, owned network — no accelerator merchant margin on inference. Combined with collapsing cost-per-token and better intent capture on commercial queries, the 'inference destroys the margin' path runs through the company least exposed to it.

**The bear misreads the agent signals he calls warnings.** Sentiment's emitted signal is *strong_buy*; Technical's is *buy*. The lone sell is Macro/FX — medium confidence, based on a 9-of-18 split committee (a tie, not a hawkish majority), and explicitly self-reversing on a Fed pivot to cuts in late 2026.

Now finish the calculation he stopped at: the same $4.2T at a forward P/E of 23.33x implies roughly **$180B of forward earnings — a 26% decline in earnings power that consensus has already written down**. So when he says "his bear case does not actually contain an earnings decline," he is wrong about whose case contains it. The market's case contains it. It is sitting in his star exhibit. My downside does not require me to forecast an earnings decline, because the sell-side he keeps citing at 58-to-6 has already forecast one — and *still* only gets to a 23x multiple on the depressed number. That is the whole trade: you are paying a premium multiple on trough earnings, and being told the trough is a gift.

**Then the pincer.** He explains the 30% cash conversion ($73.3B FCF on $243B net income) as "capex is consuming two-thirds of the engine right now." Fine — then the implied spend is on the order of $150–170B annually, and depreciation on that base does not produce a one-year 26% EPS dip that then reverses; it produces a multi-year, compounding, non-cash charge that grinds through the P&L for the entire useful life of the assets, while the assets themselves need replacing on a 3–5 year AI-hardware cycle. Alternatively, capex is *not* the whole gap — in which case the $243B of "trailing earnings" is inflated by non-cash items (equity-stake marks, tax discretes), the 17.27x "cheap" multiple is measuring earnings that never became cash, and the 23.33x forward figure is simply the honest multiple. He must pick one, and both branches are bearish. He cannot have a modest, self-reversing capex dip *and* a capex program large enough to explain a 70% cash-conversion shortfall. On "normalize capex and the yield triples": you may only add back *growth* capex. Every dollar Alphabet is spending on inference infrastructure is being spent to keep queries it already owns from migrating to an answer engine. Spending required to hold existing share is maintenance capex by definition, and maintenance capex is never added back. And the vertical-integration defense inverts: owning the TPUs and the data centers converts a supplier's variable margin into *your* fixed asset base and *your* depreciation schedule. A firm renting compute can stop renting. Alphabet cannot un-build a data center if monetization per answer lands 20% light. That is operating leverage in reverse, and it is precisely why the forward multiple expanded.

**On the macro and the consensus, two corrections of fact.** He asserts "we are in late 2026" as though the Macro/FX agent's reversal trigger has fired. It is August. The pivot is a forecast, not an event, and the agent's own text conditions the reversal on cuts that have not happened. Worse, the asymmetry runs against him: rate cuts are already substantially embedded in a 23x forward multiple on a 1.24-beta mega-cap index heavyweight — the pivot is the *bull* case being paid for in advance, while a split committee (his framing, not mine) leaving nine officials projecting tightening is a live, unhedged tail. And his treatment of the Sentiment agent remains a category error. He says the *label* is strong_buy, filed at **medium** confidence, while the *reasoning* says sentiment "may be ahead of fundamentals" with "minimal margin for disappointment" and instructs the reader to watch for reversal. When the label and the analysis disagree, the analysis is the information. In a debate about what is priced in, 90.6% bullish with **zero** sell ratings is not 58 votes of validation — it is proof there is no marginal buyer left and no downgrade already absorbed. Regulation is not "priced" because analysts acknowledged it; it is unpriced precisely because not one of them will underwrite the downside in a rating. Meanwhile the technical floor is a single line: lose the 200-day at $329.83 — with price already 3.18% *below* the 50-day and momentum merely "emerging" — and the only thing left is a multiple opinion in a stock where the multiple is the entire argument.
key_points: The bull's own arithmetic contains the earnings decline he says my case lacks: $4.2T at 17.27x trailing implies ~$243B net income; at 23.33x forward implies ~$180B — consensus has already marked earnings power down ~26%, and still only pays 23x for it.

The 30% cash conversion is a pincer, not a bull point: either capex is ~$150-170B (a multi-year compounding depreciation drag on 3-5 year hardware cycles, not a one-year dip), or trailing 'earnings' are inflated by non-cash items and the cheap 17.27x multiple is fiction. Both branches are bearish.
Capex spent to stop existing queries migrating to answer engines is maintenance capex, not growth capex — you cannot add it back to manufacture a 5% normalized FCF yield.

Owning TPUs and data centers converts a supplier's variable margin into Alphabet's fixed asset base and fixed depreciation schedule — that is operating leverage in reverse, and it is the mechanism producing the forward multiple expansion.

The macro asymmetry is inverted: Fed cuts are already embedded in a 23x forward multiple on a 1.24-beta index heavyweight (it is August, not 'late 2026' — the pivot has not happened), while nine officials projecting tightening is an unhedged tail.

Zero sell ratings out of 64 is not validation that regulation is priced — it is evidence that no downgrade has been absorbed and no marginal buyer remains; the Sentiment agent's own reasoning, at medium confidence, says sentiment is ahead of fundamentals.

No sell-side cohort in history has rated a stock near-unanimous buy into a modeled 26% EPS collapse. The bear has not discovered a hidden consensus forecast; he has discovered that trailing P/E and forward P/E are computed off different numerators — GAAP net income including non-operating and equity-mark gains versus estimated forward operating EPS. He then built a fork ("either capex explains the cash gap, or trailing earnings are inflated — both are bearish") that conveniently omits the only number immune to it: **$73.3B of free cash flow is measured after capex and after every accounting convention he is arguing about.** Cash is cash. Whichever branch of his fork is true, the cash engine generating $73.3B *while* funding the largest infrastructure build-out in corporate history is unchanged, unlevered, and undiluted.

That is not a defensive moat expenditure; it is fungible capacity with an external bid. Which also dissolves his "you cannot un-build a data center" point: if monetization per answer lands light, that silicon does not become a stranded asset, it gets sold as Cloud compute at market rates. Compare the counterfactual he prefers — renting from Nvidia and a hyperscaler — where you pay a supplier's margin forever, on someone else's schedule, with no residual asset and no ability to redirect. Alphabet designs its own TPUs, owns its own fiber, and runs its own data centers. In a world where inference is the new marginal cost of search, being the only search-scale player that does not pay a merchant margin on every accelerator is not a liability. It is the entire reason the 32.8% net margin has a path to surviving the transition.

Against it: normalized cash conversion toward this company's historical 65–75% range, Cloud inflecting, Gemini monetization optionality that no 23x multiple prices, and a self-funded platform transition that maybe three companies on earth could execute. Size it, respect $329.83 as the invalidation, and buy the dip in an intact uptrend.

Take him at his word, because I think he is largely right. Then say out loud what follows: **the 17.27x trailing multiple is not a valuation of the business.** It is a valuation of GAAP net income inflated by equity marks and tax discretes that will never recur and never become cash. Strip them, and the honest multiple on the operating engine is the forward one — 23.33x — for a mega-cap facing, in the Fundamentals agent's own words, "real" regulatory and AI-competition headwinds. Every "you're paying 17.3x for the best franchise in the world" sentence in rounds one through three is now withdrawn by its author. He had exactly two assets: a cheap trailing multiple and a unanimous sell side. He spent the first to defend the second. And the second is not evidence at all: 58 buys, 6 holds, **zero** sells is a distribution with no variance, which is another way of saying it carries no information. He deploys it circularly — zero sells proves regulation is priced, and zero sells proves earnings can't fall — when a rating is not a risk underwriting. The Sentiment agent, filing at only *medium* confidence, says the quiet part: "sentiment may be ahead of fundamentals," "minimal margin for disappointment," monitor for *reversal*.

**The Cloud-fungibility defense is the bear case wearing a suit.** He rescues the capex from my maintenance-capex objection by declaring the same silicon is Google Cloud's physical plant with "an external bid," and adds that if answer-monetization lands light, the hardware "gets sold as Cloud compute at market rates." Follow the money that implies: search dollars earned at a 32.8% net margin with near-zero marginal cost are being converted into rented compute sold into a market that includes AWS, Azure, and every neocloud, on a depreciating 3–5 year asset base. That is not moat defense — that is a **mix shift down the margin curve**, and it is exactly why the forward multiple sits above the trailing one. Note also that he cannot have it both ways on the add-back: if this capex is generating third-party Cloud revenue, it is growth capex whose revenue is *already in the numbers* at Cloud's margin, so "normalize capex and the FCF yield triples" is off the table; if it is defending queries Alphabet already owns, it is maintenance capex and never adds back. He has argued both in consecutive paragraphs. And "market rates" is doing enormous work: TPUs are proprietary silicon in a CUDA-standard developer world — the pool of third parties who can absorb that capacity at premium rates is precisely the pool Alphabet is trying to sell to, in a build-out cycle where the entire industry is adding capacity simultaneously. Residual value at market rates in a shortage is a very different number from residual value at market rates in a glut, and the glut is the scenario in which you'd need to sell. Meanwhile the $73.3B he calls "immune to accounting" is immune in both directions: it is a **1.74% cash yield** on the asset — the honest, post-capex, post-convention return an owner actually receives — offered against a policy rate environment where nine of eighteen officials still project tightening and, on his own admission, the pivot has not fired.

**What finally settles it is the shape of the payoff, and the bull's own risk instruction.** At 23x forward on trough-ish operating EPS, with zero sell ratings outstanding and a 1.74% cash yield, upside requires a *re-rating* — a Fed pivot, Gemini monetization nobody has demonstrated, Cloud inflection — while downside requires only the **absence of good news**. That is not a 1.237 beta cutting symmetrically; it is a coiled multiple on one of the largest index weights in existence, where the marginal buyer is passive flow rather than a valuation-sensitive investor. My downside is bounded and specific: a derate to 18x forward on flat EPS is roughly **−23%**; pair it with a 10% earnings miss from distribution remedies or ad-slot compression in answer-format search and you are near **−30%**, with the only visible support a single line at the 200-day MA of $329.83 — which price is approaching from *below* the 50-day (−3.18%) on merely "emerging" momentum, with a "volume washout" that is equally consistent with buyer absence. And notice the bull's closing advice: "respect $329.83 as the invalidation." That is a confession that this thesis has **no valuation floor** — only a chart line. A position whose risk control is a stop-loss on a 1.24-beta index heavyweight is a position that will be sold into correlated forced liquidation, at the worst price, precisely when the macro agent's tail fires. I am not arguing Alphabet is a bad company; it is a superb one, which is why the market has already paid for the superb part. I am arguing you are being asked to accept equity risk — regulatory, margin-structural, and duration — for a 1.7% cash yield and a multiple that only works if a self-funded platform transition nobody has completed lands on time. **Wait. There is no scarcity in a $4.2T market cap.** What would change my mind: a demonstrated monetization rate per AI answer at or above legacy SERP RPM, capex plateauing with cash conversion recovering toward 65%, and a resolved search-distribution remedy. None of those is in this report set. Until then: avoid, and let the 23x multiple prove itself first.

Whether the 30% cash conversion is a temporary distortion that normalizes toward 65–75% (bull) or evidence of a permanent, compounding cost base on a 3–5 year replacement cycle (bear).

Vertical integration: a structural cost advantage that preserves the 32.8% margin through the transition (bull) vs. reverse operating leverage — you cannot un-build a data center — plus proprietary TPUs in a CUDA-standard world with weak residual value in a glut (bear).
AI answer-format monetization: higher intent capture and better ad relevance on commercial queries (bull) vs. fewer ad slots and an unproven RPM (bear). Both concede this is interpretation, not data.

How to read the Sentiment agent: the label is strong_buy, and the caveats are a risk annotation on a bullish call (bull) vs. when label and reasoning conflict, the reasoning is the information (bear).

Whether a chart-line stop is adequate risk control (bull: defined risk) or a confession that the thesis has no valuation floor and will be sold into correlated forced liquidation (bear).
Beta 1.237: leverage in both directions (bull) vs. duration risk that reprices first when discount rates move (bear).
